title: Wedge problems and dispersive shock waves in the two-dimensional Toda lattice
authors: Marco Calabrese, Gino Biondini, Christopher Chong, Panayotis Kevrekidis
abstract: We study the formation and interaction of dispersive shock waves (DSWs) in the two-dimensional Toda lattice subject to wedge-type initial conditions, and show that their interaction gives rise to a discrete analog of Mach reflection for dispersive shock waves in discrete systems. The initial jump across each leg of the wedge acts locally as a Riemann problem for the one-dimensional Toda lattice, producing two oblique DSWs whose leading-edge soliton amplitude is determined explicitly by the one-dimensional Whitham modulation theory. The two-dimensional nature of the problem manifests when these oblique DSWs meet along the symmetry axis. We show that, for compressive wedges (i.e., when the initial conditions are such that two oblique DSWs that are generated propagate toward each other), a critical slope $q_{\mathrm{cr}}$ separates two regimes: in the subcritical regime ($q<q_{\mathrm{cr}}$) the interaction is resonant and it produces an expanding DSW whose amplitude, length and velocity are explicitly computed by using exact soliton solutions of the two-dimensional Toda lattice; in the supercritical regime ($q>q_{\mathrm{cr}}$) the interaction is ordinary and produces a localized peak whose amplitude is determined analytically. We also show qualitatively that a similar dichotomy between two regimes exists for expansive wedges (i.e., when the initial conditions are such that the two oblique DSWs propagate away from each other). We confirm all analytical predictions by comparing them with the results of direct numerical simulations. Finally, we show that the continuum limit of the result is consistent with the analogous theory for the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation, providing an independent validation of the analytical framework.
summary: This paper analyzes dispersive shock wave formation in the 2D Toda lattice using wedge-type initial conditions. The key finding is that the interaction of these waves exhibits a discrete Mach reflection, characterized by a critical slope that separates resonant (expanding) from ordinary (localized peak) interaction regimes. The work provides a rigorous analytical framework validated against numerical simulations and the KP equation.
main_problem: The study investigates the formation and interaction of Dispersive Shock Waves (DSWs) within the framework of the two-dimensional Toda lattice (2DTL) when subjected to wedge-type initial conditions.
main_result: The interaction of the generated oblique DSWs yields a discrete analog of Mach reflection, with the dynamics bifurcating into resonant (expanding DSW) and ordinary (localized peak) regimes depending on a critical slope parameter $q_{cr}$.
method: The analysis uses local reduction to the one-dimensional Toda lattice (Riemann problem) and employs Whitham modulation theory to determine soliton amplitudes, validating results against numerical simulations and the continuum KP equation limit.
model_or_system: The primary model is the two-dimensional Toda lattice (2DTL), described by a specific non-linear partial difference equation. The system is initialized with wedge-type conditions defined by a slope parameter $q$.
key_observables: The amplitude, length, and velocity of the resulting DSWs, and the existence of a critical slope $q_{cr}$ separating dynamic regimes.
important_parameters: The slope parameter $q$ defining the wedge geometry, and the critical slope $q_{cr}$ which dictates the nature of the wave interaction.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of Whitham modulation theory and relies on the consistency between the discrete 2DTL results and the continuum limit theory for the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili (KP) equation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the geometrically distinct initial data for Type I and Type II wedges. Later figures show density plots illustrating the formation of tilted stems in asymmetric subcritical/supercritical regimes.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the 1D Toda lattice Riemann problem to the 2D DSW interaction in the 2DTL. It classifies dynamics based on wedge type (I/II) and parameter regimes (sub/supercritical), deriving explicit analytical solutions for the resulting wave structures.
why_interesting: While the core physics is in nonlinear wave dynamics, the mathematical techniques—such as the use of integrable systems (Toda lattice) and modulation theory—are highly relevant to understanding complex, non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body quantum systems.

Top row: type I wedges, with q = 0.4 (subcritical, left) and q = 1.8 (supercritical, right). Bottom row: type II wedges, with q = −0.4 (subcritical, left) and q = −1.8 (supercritical, right). The gold line marks the wedge boundary at the slope q of each panel; the angle β formed with the y−axis which satisfies β = arctanq is indicated in each panel. The vertical dashed line marks n = 0. The white dash-dotted lines correspond to the critical slope |q| = qcr ≈1.429 from Eq. (4.10) separating the subcritical and supercritical regimes.

Figure 2: The three types of elastic two-soliton solutions of the 2DTL (index pairs as labeled), with phase parameters (P1,P2,P3,P4) = (−2.3,−0.69,0.69,2.71), as in [14]. Columns, from left to right: ordinary, resonant, and asymmetric interactions. Rows: earlier and later snapshots (top row: t = 4; bottom row: t = 10), illustrating the temporal evolution of each solution type. In the resonant interaction (center column), the pair of Y-junctions mediating the stem visibly separates further between the two snapshots.
